subject: business-studies
title: Startup Stretch Adventure
welcome_lead: Exam-style stretch. Justify a legal structure, weigh up sources of finance and analyse aims trade-offs.
meta_desc: GCSE Business Studies stretch — evaluating legal structures, finance sources and conflicting business aims.
final_note: You can now justify a choice of legal structure, recommend a source of finance with reasoning, and analyse conflicting aims.

concepts.def: Any group affected by or affecting the business
Owner of one or more shares in a company
A share of profit paid out to shareholders
Profit kept in the business to reinvest
Short-term aim to stay trading, esp. for startups
A firm's sales as % of total market sales

walkthroughs.body_html:
Pick the structure that fits the risk and ambition.

Low risk + small scale = sole trader. Want to raise £millions = PLC. Want limited liability but keep control = Ltd.

A bank loan keeps ownership but adds interest costs. Selling shares brings cash with no repayment, but you lose control.

Evaluate by matching the source to the stage and goal of the firm.

Aims can clash: chasing growth may reduce short-term profit (you reinvest instead of paying dividends).

Pursuing social/ethical aims can raise costs but build brand loyalty.

mcqs.q: Which is most likely a SHORT-TERM aim of a new startup?
options: Become a multinational
Survival
Dominate the global market
Acquire competitors

mcqs.q: Selling new shares to investors will most likely cause.
options: An increase in interest payments
A loss of owner control
A rise in fixed assets only
A drop in liabilities

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a stakeholder and a shareholder?
options: Stakeholders and shareholders are different spellings of the same word.
Stakeholders are managers and shareholders are workers.
A shareholder owns shares in the company; a stakeholder is anyone affected by or with interest in the business — employees, customers, suppliers, community, plus shareholders.
Profit is what businesses earn; revenue is what employees earn.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between profit and revenue?
options: Revenue is total income from sales (price x quantity sold); profit is revenue minus total costs — what is left after paying for everything.
Profit and revenue are different words for the same thing.
Profitable businesses fail only when employees steal.
Profit is what businesses earn; revenue is what employees earn.

mcqs.q: Why can a profitable business still fail?
options: If a business is profitable it cannot run out of money.
Because cash flow and profit are different — a business may be profitable on paper but run out of cash to pay bills, especially if customers owe money or stock ties up funds.
Profit is what businesses earn; revenue is what employees earn.
Profitable businesses fail only when employees steal.
